cards.s: Tests with pytest
cards.html:
Chapter 3 · Level 1: Tests and Your First Pipeline. A pipeline can only be as good as the checks it runs. In this level you set up the running example, learn pytest from zero, and let GitHub Actions run your tests on every push.

After this level you can:

  • Set up a Python project with uv, a src/ layout and pyproject.toml.
  • Write tests with assertions, fixtures, parametrize and pytest.raises, and decide what to test in an ML project.
  • Write a GitHub Actions workflow and explain every line of it.
  • Read a failing run, fix it, and show the status with a badge.

What you build: The credit-api repository on GitHub with 31 tests and a workflow that runs them on every push and pull request.

cards.s: The running example: credit-api
cards.html:
credit-api predicts whether a loan applicant is a good or bad credit risk. It uses the public German Credit dataset (1,000 applicants, from the University of Hamburg, via the UCI/OpenML repositories), reduced to eight features, a scikit-learn gradient-boosting model, and a FastAPI service. The model is deliberately small so that training takes about one second, which is what makes training inside CI realistic.

project layout:

cards.s: The running example: credit-api
cards.html:
credit-api/
├── pyproject.toml          # project metadata, dependencies, tool config
├── uv.lock                 # exact versions of every package (commit it!)
├── data/german_credit.csv  # 1,000 rows, committed: small and public
├── src/credit_api/
│   ├── config.py           # paths and column names
│   ├── data.py             # load + stratified sample
│   ├── validation.py       # data contract (Level 4)
│   ├── model.py            # the sklearn pipeline
│   ├── train.py            # train, save model, write metrics
│   ├── gate.py             # quality gate (Level 4)
│   ├── schemas.py          # API request/response models
│   └── app.py              # FastAPI app
├── tests/                  # one test file per module
└── .github/workflows/      # CI/CD definitions

Concept: Why the src/ layout

With code under src/, Python can only import your package after it has been installed (which uv sync does). Tests therefore run against the installed package, exactly like production, and you cannot accidentally import a file that is missing from the package.

cards.s: uv, the virtual environment and the lock file
cards.html:
uv replaces pip, venv and pip-tools with one fast tool. Install it once (curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh, or brew install uv), then:

terminal:

git clone https://github.com/<you>/credit-api && cd credit-api
uv sync                     # creates .venv, installs exactly uv.lock
uv run pytest               # runs pytest inside .venv
uv add scikit-learn         # add a dependency (updates pyproject + lock)
uv add --group dev pytest   # add a development-only dependency

The lock file uv.lock records the exact version of every package, including dependencies of dependencies. Your laptop, CI and the Docker image all install from it, so "works on my machine" problems disappear. uv sync --locked (used in CI) refuses to run if pyproject.toml and uv.lock disagree. The project file:

pyproject.toml:

cards.s: uv, the virtual environment and the lock file
cards.html:
[project]
name = "credit-api"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Credit-risk model served with FastAPI (CI/CD tutorial)"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = [
    "fastapi>=0.115",
    "uvicorn>=0.30",
    "scikit-learn>=1.5",
    "pandas>=2.2",
    "joblib>=1.4",
]

[dependency-groups]
train = ["pandera>=0.20"]
tracking = ["mlflow>=3.0"]
dev = [
    { include-group = "train" },
    "pytest>=8.3",
    "pytest-cov>=5.0",
    "httpx2>=2.0",
    "ruff>=0.6",
    "mypy>=1.11",
    "pandas-stubs>=2.2",
    "pre-commit>=3.8",
]

[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
testpaths = ["tests"]

cards.s: uv, the virtual environment and the lock file
cards.html: Runtime dependencies go into dependencies; tools only needed during development and training go into dependency groups. The Docker image later installs only the runtime part, which keeps it small. The rest of pyproject.toml configures pytest, coverage, ruff and mypy, so all settings live in one file.

cards.s: pytest from zero
cards.html:
pytest finds files named test_*.py, runs every function whose name starts with test_, and reports each as passed or failed. A test is just a function with assert statements; when an assertion is false, pytest shows you the values involved.

tests/test_data.py:

def test_no_duplicate_rows(df: pd.DataFrame) -> None:
    assert df.duplicated().sum() == 0

def test_missing_column_is_reported(tmp_path) -> None:
    bad = tmp_path / "bad.csv"
    bad.write_text("duration,age\n12,30\n")
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="missing columns"):
        load_data(bad)

cards.s: pytest from zero
cards.html: These two tests show the two basic patterns: check a value (assert ... == 0) and check that something fails correctly (with pytest.raises(ValueError, match=...)). tmp_path is a built-in fixture: pytest gives the test a fresh temporary directory.

cards.s: Fixtures: shared setup
cards.html:
A fixture is a function that prepares something a test needs. Tests request it by naming it as a parameter. Fixtures in tests/conftest.py are available to all test files:

tests/conftest.py:

cards.s: Fixtures: shared setup
cards.html:
"""Shared fixtures. pytest discovers this file automatically."""

from collections.abc import Iterator
from pathlib import Path

import joblib
import pandas as pd
import pytest
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

from credit_api.data import load_data
from credit_api.lineage import write_meta

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def df() -> pd.DataFrame:
    return load_data()

@pytest.fixture
def applicant() -> dict[str, object]:
    return {
        "checking_status": "<0",
        "duration": 24,
        "credit_history": "existing paid",
        "purpose": "new car",
        "credit_amount": 4000,
        "savings_status": "<100",
        "employment": "1<=X<4",
        "age": 35,
    }

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def model_file(tmp_path_factory: pytest.TempPathFactory) -> Path:
    """Train a tiny model once per test session (fast: ~1 s)."""
    from credit_api.train import train

    model, _ = train(sample_frac=0.3, max_iter=20)
    path = tmp_path_factory.mktemp("models") / "model.joblib"
    joblib.dump(model, path)
    write_meta(path, {"model_version": "test-1", "data_sha256": "ab" * 32})
    return path

@pytest.fixture
def client(
    model_file: Path, monkeypatch: pytest.MonkeyPatch
) -> Iterator[TestClient]:
    monkeypatch.setenv("MODEL_PATH", str(model_file))
    from credit_api.app import app

cards.s: Fixtures: shared setup
cards.html: Three things to notice. scope="session" (line 14) loads the CSV once for the whole run instead of once per test. The model_file fixture (line 34) trains a tiny model (30 % of the data, 20 trees) once per session, so the API tests have a real model in about one second. And client (line 45) uses monkeypatch, another built-in fixture, to set an environment variable only for the duration of one test.

cards.s: Parametrize: one test, many cases
cards.html:
tests/test_data.py:

@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    ("column", "value"),
    [("age", 12), ("duration", 0), ("credit_amount", -5), ("target", 2)],
)
def test_contract_rejects_bad_values(
    df: pd.DataFrame, column: str, value: int
) -> None:
    broken = df.copy()
    broken.loc[0, column] = value
    with pytest.raises(pandera.errors.SchemaErrors):
        validate(broken)

pytest runs this function four times and reports each case separately, e.g. test_contract_rejects_bad_values[age-12]. Use parametrize whenever you are tempted to copy-paste a test.

cards.s: Reading a failure, and comparing floats
cards.html:
pytest rewrites assert statements so that a failure shows the values on both sides. Run this small file (it is not part of credit-api; put it in a scratch folder):

test_demo.py:

import pytest

def test_float_naive():
    assert 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3

def test_float_approx():
    assert 0.1 + 0.2 == pytest.approx(0.3)

expected output:

    def test_float_naive():
>       assert 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3
E       assert (0.1 + 0.2) == 0.3

test_demo.py:6: AssertionError
FAILED test_demo.py::test_float_naive - assert (0.1 + 0.2) == 0.3

cards.s: Reading a failure, and comparing floats
cards.html: The > marks the failing line, E lines explain it. Here the values look equal, but 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 in binary floating point. In ML code you compare floats all the time (metrics, probabilities, scaled features), so learn the tool for it: pytest.approx(0.3) accepts a relative difference of 1e-6 by default; pytest.approx(0.786, abs=0.01) sets an absolute tolerance. It also works on lists, dicts and NumPy arrays: assert probs == pytest.approx([0.2, 0.8]). For DataFrames use pandas.testing.assert_frame_equal, which shows which cells differ.

cards.s: Fixtures in depth: scope, teardown, and a trap
cards.html:
A fixture can do cleanup after the test. Write yield instead of return: everything after yield runs when the test is finished, even if it failed.

a fixture with teardown:

@pytest.fixture
def db_conn():
    conn = connect("postgresql://localhost/test")   # setup
    yield conn                                      # the test runs here
    conn.close()                                    # teardown, always

The scope decides how often the fixture runs: function (default, once per test), module (once per file), session (once per run). Wider scopes are faster but shared, which leads to the most confusing kind of test failure.

What if… a test passes alone but fails when the whole suite runs?

cards.s: Fixtures in depth: scope, teardown, and a trap
cards.html:
What happens: Real output from a two-test file that shares a session-scoped DataFrame fixture:

df =    age  income       ratio
0   30    3000  100.000000
1   45    5200  115.555556

    def test_b_expects_raw_columns(df):
>       assert list(df.columns) == ["age", "income"]
E       AssertionError: assert ['age', 'income', 'ratio'] == ['age',
E         'income']
E         Left contains one more item: 'ratio'

Run alone (pytest test_demo.py::test_b_expects_raw_columns), the same test passes.

Why: test_a added a column to the DataFrame. With scope="session", test_b received the same object, already modified. The result depends on test order, which is why it can be green on your laptop and red in CI (or after adding a test).

cards.s: Fixtures in depth: scope, teardown, and a trap
cards.html: What you do: Never mutate a shared fixture. Copy inside the test (df = df.copy()), or give the fixture the default function scope. Our credit-api fixture df is session-scoped for speed, so tests that change data call .copy() first. To find order dependence on purpose, the plugin pytest-randomly shuffles the test order on every run.

cards.s: Isolating external calls: monkeypatch and mocks
cards.html:
Unit tests must not call the network: it is slow, costs money, and fails when the other service is down. Replace the call during the test. monkeypatch swaps an attribute and restores it afterwards:

patterns (sketch):

from credit_api import app as app_module

def test_health_reports_version(client, monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setattr(app_module, "APP_VERSION", "abc123")
    assert client.get("/health").json()["version"] == "abc123"

def test_llm_failure_is_handled(monkeypatch):
    def boom(*args, **kwargs):
        raise TimeoutError("LLM did not answer")

    monkeypatch.setattr("rag_api.llm.ClaudeGenerator.generate", boom)
    ...  # assert that your code returns a clear 503, not a crash

cards.s: Isolating external calls: monkeypatch and mocks
cards.html: For "was it called, and with what?" use unittest.mock.Mock, whose .assert_called_once_with(...) checks the arguments. The cleaner alternative, used in rag-api (Level 4), is dependency injection: code receives a client object, and tests pass a fake class. No patching needed.

cards.s: Testing the API
cards.html:
FastAPI's TestClient calls your endpoints in-process, without starting a server:

tests/test_api.py:

def test_predict_returns_probability(client: TestClient, applicant) -> None:
    r = client.post("/predict", json=applicant)
    assert r.status_code == 200
    body = r.json()
    assert body["risk"] in {"good", "bad"}
    assert 0.0 <= body["probability_bad"] <= 1.0

def test_predict_validates_input(client: TestClient, applicant) -> None:
    applicant["age"] = 7
    r = client.post("/predict", json=applicant)
    assert r.status_code == 422  # FastAPI's "unprocessable entity"

The 422 test is easy to forget but valuable: it proves that input validation works, i.e. that a nonsense request is rejected with a clear error instead of producing a nonsense prediction.

cards.s: What to test in an ML project
cards.html:
Test typeExamples in credit-api
Data loading & contractmissing columns raise an error; values in valid ranges; no duplicate rows (test_data.py)
Pre-processingstratified sampling keeps the class balance; unknown categories do not crash (handle_unknown="ignore")
Model behaviouroutput shape, probabilities in [0, 1], determinism with a fixed seed (test_model.py)
Quality gate logicthe gate fails below a floor and on a regression (test_gate.py)
APIhealth check, valid prediction, 422 on bad input, 503 when no model is loaded (test_api.py)

cards.s: Behavioural tests: properties of a good model
cards.html:
You cannot assert that the model predicts exactly 0.6427. You can assert properties that any sensible credit model must have. These are the tests in tests/test_behaviour.py:

tests/test_behaviour.py:

def test_beats_random_guessing(model, df: pd.DataFrame) -> None:
    proba = model.predict_proba(df[FEATURES])[:, 1]
    assert roc_auc_score(df[TARGET], proba) > 0.6

def test_column_order_does_not_matter(model, df: pd.DataFrame) -> None:
    rows = df[FEATURES].head(20)
    shuffled = rows[list(reversed(FEATURES))]
    a = model.predict_proba(rows)[:, 1]
    b = model.predict_proba(shuffled)[:, 1]
    assert a == pytest.approx(b)

def test_input_is_not_modified(model, df: pd.DataFrame) -> None:
    rows = df[FEATURES].head(5).copy()
    before = rows.copy()
    model.predict_proba(rows)
    pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(rows, before)

def test_no_overlap_between_train_and_test(df: pd.DataFrame) -> None:
    train_idx, test_idx = train_test_split(
        df.index, test_size=0.25, stratify=df[TARGET], random_state=SEED
    )
    assert set(train_idx).isdisjoint(test_idx)

@pytest.mark.parametrize("delta", [1, -1])
def test_small_age_change_small_effect(
    model, applicant: dict[str, object], delta: int
) -> None:
    row = pd.DataFrame([applicant])[FEATURES]
    moved = row.copy()
    moved["age"] = moved["age"] + delta
    p0 = model.predict_proba(row)[0, 1]
    p1 = model.predict_proba(moved)[0, 1]
    assert abs(p1 - p0) < 0.10

cards.s: Behavioural tests: properties of a good model
cards.html:
Each test guards against a specific, real failure:

TestCatches
beats_random_guessingA pipeline that trains on shuffled labels or the wrong target column: everything runs, AUC ≈ 0.5. We measured: a "predict the average" dummy model scores exactly 0.50 here.
column_order_does_not_matterTraining–serving skew: the API builds the row with columns in a different order than training. Our pipeline selects columns by name, so this passes; a model fed with a NumPy array by position would silently mix up age and duration.
input_is_not_modifiedPre-processing that changes the caller's DataFrame in place, a classic source of order-dependent bugs.
no_overlap_between_train_and_testData leakage: if test rows are also in training, every metric is too optimistic and the gate is meaningless.
small_age_change_small_effectAn unstable model, or a feature accidentally used on the wrong scale: one year of age should not swing the probability by 10 points.

cards.s: Behavioural tests: properties of a good model
cards.html:
Watch out: Behavioural tests need honest tolerances

The 0.6 and 0.10 limits were chosen to be clearly true for any reasonable model, not tuned to today's numbers. Avoid tests that break whenever you retrain ("probability for applicant X is between 0.63 and 0.65"): they fail for good changes, and people learn to update the numbers without thinking. Directional expectations ("a longer loan should not lower the risk") are tempting but often false for tree models on small data; check them on many rows and test a share ("holds for ≥ 90 % of applicants") rather than every row.

Watch out: Keep tests fast and deterministic

cards.s: Behavioural tests: properties of a good model
cards.html:
A test suite that takes ten minutes will be skipped by humans. Train on small samples, use fixed seeds (random_state=42), and mark slow tests with @pytest.mark.slow so that pytest -m "not slow" gives quick feedback. Never call external APIs or real databases in unit tests; use fakes (you will see this with the RAG service in Level 4).

cards.s: Behavioural tests: properties of a good model
cards.html:
(test_operations.py belongs to Chapter 7; ignore it for now.) The flags you will use every day:

CommandUse it when
pytest -xStop at the first failure.
pytest --lfRe-run only the tests that failed last time.
pytest -k gateRun tests whose name contains "gate".
pytest -m "not slow"Skip tests marked slow.
pytest -vvFull names and complete diffs of long values.
pytest -sShow print() output (normally captured).
pytest --pdbOpen the debugger at the failing line.
pytest --durations=5List the five slowest tests: start here when the suite gets slow.
